item.title: The Rosy Path Ahead for Your Attachment Style
item.description:
Attachment

The Rosy Path Ahead for Your Attachment Style

New relationship research shows how your attachment styles can change.

Posted August 11, 2026

Key points
  • Attachment style captures an individual’s ability to feel close to others without fearing abandonment.
  • New research shows that, across the years of adulthood most people are securely attached but there are risks.
  • Finding security and feelings of well-being in your relationships help lead the way to a fulfilling future.

A basic concept in the field of adult relationships is that it is actually the ones you had as a child which set the stage for your future. According to the theory of attachment styles, you carry with you an inner model of what relationships look like based on how your own parents or other caregivers raised you. If all is well, you’ll be “securely” attached, meaning that you're more likely to feel you can rely on others. If not, you’ll be more likely to struggle with feeling that others might abandon you or fail to deserve your trust.

Betty was raised in a household where she could never feel certain that either parent would provide emotional support. They would often criticize her harshly for failing to meet their standards. At other times, they lavished praise on her and gave her everything she wanted. It’s no wonder that, as an adult, she is constantly testing the people close to her to see which direction the relationship might take.

A Lifespan Approach to Attachment Style

From a lifespan perspective, the issues that Betty is facing could be seen as having the potential to change over time. Although an insecure attachment style could serve as an impossible obstacle, maybe there is hope, given the right circumstances. This is the approach offered by Copenhagen University Hospital’s Sebastian Simonsen and colleagues (2026) in a new study examining age differences in attachment style over the adult years (18-79). With data from nearly 3,600 Danish adults, the authors asked the question of whether there are consistent patterns across older and younger groups.

A secondary but equally important question the authors addressed was whether attachment style would play a role in predicting an individual’s mental health. People with secure attachment should, they predicted, also have higher levels of well-being and lower levels of psychological symptoms. Thus, attachment style’s relationship to age is more than an academic question; it can have practical consequences for people’s levels of depression and anxiety. In part, these associations could reflect the tendency for securely attached people to be in more satisfying relationships.

Measuring Attachment Style Over the Years

It would be ideal if the Danish study used a longitudinal design where the same people were followed over time, but instead, they only had cross-sectional data at their disposal (i.e., comparing different ages). It’s important to keep this in mind when looking at the findings. On the positive side, the sample was large and the data were carried out over two successive periods (2020 and 2021), so that the findings weren’t specific just to one time of testing.

The attachment questionnaire the authors used is a standard instrument in which participants rate whether each of four attachment “prototypes” applies to them or not. They fell into four categories: secure, fearful (afraid of becoming close), dismissive (avoidant and withdrawing), and preoccupied (afraid of being abandoned). The secure attachment prototype read as follows:

It is easy for me to become emotionally close to others. I am comfortable depending on others and having others depend on me. I don’t worry about being alone and having others accept me.

Overall, there was good news in the data in that 65% of the population reported that they were securely attached. This is a figure that is consistent with those emerging from other studies of adult attachment styles, especially in wealthy countries such as Denmark.

Adjusting for such factors as year, marital status, and gender, the findings showed clear improvements across age groups in terms of secure attachment, with 20% more in the 50-59 age group being more likely to report “yes” to the secure attachment prototype. Younger age groups also had higher levels of attachment anxiety as indicated by the preoccupied and fearful categories. The findings also supported the positive association between secure attachment and mental health, as was predicted.

Standing out from these overall positive age trends was the fact that people 70-79 had higher levels of dismissive attachment. Although this could reflect the possibility of some type of cohort effect (i.e., something specific to this group of 70+ people), Simonsen et al. note that this finding is consistent with other cross-sectional research going back as far as 1998.

Let’s pause and look at this finding for the oldest age group, which, again, was not just specific to this study. Overall, across the whole sample, only 14% endorsed the dismissive prototype, so the actual numbers are small. However, the fact that 22% of the oldest group did suggests that there may be challenges older adults face when deciding on whether or how much energy to devote to relationships. It’s also possible that they have lost their spouse or life partner and are now putting their lives back together in the face of this new reality. Unfortunately, adopting a dismissive attachment style could prove to make it more challenging for these older individuals to adapt to that new reality.

Charting Your Own Path Forward

The Simonsen et al. findings are generally quite heartening in that the odds are low for having an insecure attachment style. However, if you are in your young adult years, there is a slightly greater risk that you are experiencing attachment difficulties. That people sail through to their 50s could provide you with some inspiration.

Knowing, though, that a dismissive attachment style characterized one-fifth of the oldest adults in this study, it may be worth considering how you invest your emotional energies as you move through or plan your later years. Attachment figures can take many forms other than a romantic partner. Children, grandchildren, pets, and even people you get to know in your everyday activities (a hair stylist you’re close to) can serve important functions in supporting your mental health. Narrowing the definition of an attachment figure to a romantic partner may be overly limiting and even unrealistic.

To sum up, it’s great to know your chances are good that as you navigate adulthood, you can find and enjoy relationships that are both fulfilling and sustaining.

item.title: Brain, We Need to Talk
item.description:
Self-Talk

Brain, We Need to Talk

How to change your relationship with your thoughts.

Posted August 11, 2026

Key points
  • Minds can be critical, and this is often unhelpful.
  • Cognitive fusion is when we fuse words or thoughts (or any mental activity) with the truth.
  • We can change our relationship with our thoughts rather than trying to change the thoughts.

Dear Brain,

We’ve been together a long time. Let’s face it, some of it has been really fun. You’ve taken me on adventures and encouraged me to try all sorts of wacky things. You helped me with my university work and in my job since then.

But the longer this relationship continues, the more I’ve been noticing your toxic, controlling side. The little digs you make at me to undermine my confidence. The ways you try to talk me out of doing things that would be good for me, like exercise or eating healthy. The ways you tell me not to believe kind words from others or to struggle to accept help from people who care about me.

Brains are problem-solving machines whether the problem needs solving or not
Source: Illustrated by Kalos Chan, image owned by Ben Sedley

Four months ago, my house flooded, and life has been feeling pretty damn hard for me and my family. This could have been a time when you and I pulled together and worked as a team. But, no, instead of that, you couldn’t help yourself, jumping in with criticisms and putdowns. You tell me that other people have it much worse than me and I have no right to find things hard. You tell me that I shouldn’t be still struggling this much four months later and that I’m pathetic for not having prevented things that I logically know I couldn’t have done anything about.

We’ve argued lots, but even when I try convince you that you’re wrong, you have an answer for everything. I’ve tried ignoring you, but the more I try to distract myself, the louder you attack me. I know many people have dysfunctional relationships with their brains, but that’s no comfort to me when my brain is being mean.

In acceptance and commitment therapy, this is called cognitive fusion. Fusion means sticking things together. Cognitive fusion is when I fuse words or thoughts (or any mental activity) with the truth. It’s when I act as if my thoughts are always deserving of attention and feel the emotions based on what those thoughts are telling me. When I imagine an event going badly in the future, I feel scared right now. When I remember a time I did something embarrassing in the past, I feel shame in the present. I call myself awful names or tell myself I don’t deserve care, and then I feel sad.

The opposite is cognitive defusion, seeing mental activity for what it is. My brain generates thoughts, images, memories, urges, and more, because that's its job. It’s not its job to be realistic or accurate, because overestimating risks or danger or social rejection has kept humans safe for thousands of years. But I get to choose whether I treat those thoughts as true and happening right now or if I respond to them as my brain generating lots of noise, some of which is helpful and some of which is getting in the way of me living the life I want to live.

Cognitive Defusion
Source: Illustrated by Kalos Chan, image owned by Ben Sedley

Put another way, cognitive fusion is saying: "I'm an idiot."

Cognitive defusion is: "I'm noticing that I'm having a thought that I'm an idiot."

The thought hasn't changed, but my relationship with it has.

So, I’m going to stop automatically believing you. I’m done acting as if everything you say is true. I know that we still have to work together, and when you have something helpful to say, I’ll take the advice. But when you say something that is unhelpful or rude or gets in the way of me trying to be the best me I can be, I’ll shrug off your words as ramblings from an unhelpful mind.

As the quirky comedian Emo Philips once said, “I used to think that the brain was the most wonderful organ in my body. Then I realized who was telling me this.”

item.title: Understanding Your Unique Imagination and Creative Profile
item.description:
Imagination

Understanding Your Unique Imagination and Creative Profile

Cassandra Vieten, Ph.D. on the power of imagination.

Posted August 11, 2026

Using your imagination is important for your mental health and wellbeing.

Many psychotherapy models use imagination, through visualization imagery for self-regulation, processing memories, unpacking catastrophic imaginings that induce anxiety, and employing imagery-rich metaphors. This is for good reason – imagination is a powerful tool that we can use in therapy, and in everyday life.

According to a 2023 study, a controlled, playful use of imagination can serve as a positive coping strategy during times of stress and trauma, promoting resilience (Rubinstein, D., O'Rourke, N., & Lahad, M.). But imagination is not only useful for combating mental health issues; it can also help us to succeed in reaching our goals, improving our skills, and embodying who we want to be.

Emerging research suggests that vividly imagining ourselves handling challenges, social encounters, or mastering new skills can actually enhance our performance in real life. Our imaginings have the power to ultimately shape our expectations and our choices (Dabas et al., 2025).

Cassandra Vieten, PhD, professor and research director at UC San Diego, has studied the power of imagination extensively and discovered the concept of imagination neurodiversity. She wrote the book Imagine That: Transform How You Think, Feel, and Live with the Science of Imagination to help readers better understand their own unique imagination profile and use it to their advantage. Her VISTA framework, Visualizing, Ideating, Sensing, Transforming, and Applying, offers five distinct ways of exercising the imagination.

Dr. Vieten shares her thoughts on the power of imagination in therapy and beyond.

Q: Share a bit about your background and what inspired you to write Imagine That.

Cassandra Vieten, PhD offers readers an in-depth look at the power of imagination.
Source: Victoria Pierce/Used with permission

Cassandra Vieten: I'm a clinical psychologist and professor in the Department of Family Medicine, and I direct the research at the Arthur C. Clarke Center for Human Imagination at UC San Diego. I also direct the UCSD Center for Mindfulness and serve as clinical psychology director at the Center for Psychedelic Research.

On paper, imagination might look like an unusual thing for a scientist to spend time on. I still get a version of the same reaction when people hear what I study: isn't that a little soft? Shouldn't "real" science be curing diseases and solving the climate crisis? But I have trouble thinking of anything more foundational than understanding how humans come up with original ideas and creative solutions in the first place. Imagination isn't frivolous, it's a working tool of the brain, woven into learning, foresight, empathy, and problem-solving.

The seeds of Imagine That go back much further than my research career, though. My parents had a nearly complete set of National Geographic on our shelves, and I'd get lost for hours in photographs of bioluminescent creatures in the deep sea or Aboriginal art from Australia, worlds that stretched what I believed was possible. My dad was a biochemist who used to boost me up on a stool in his lab to look at pond microbes under a microscope, so I learned early that the invisible world was every bit as full of mystery as the visible one. And my mom was a Jungian-inspired counselor who introduced me to dreams, myths, and symbols, a different kind of truth, maybe not as measurable, but very influential all the same.

Those three driving forces, the outer world, the microscopic world, and the inner world, shaped a very particular kind of imagination in me, one that leans visual and sensory and reaches for story to make sense of hard things. Fiction gave me language for something I couldn't yet name on my own. That's really the throughline of my whole career: that subjective experiences, what we imagine, the stories we tell ourselves, have real weight, real influence, and can be powerful catalysts and practices for growth and healing, or keeping us limited.

Q: What is imagination neurodiversity, and how can we better understand our unique imagination profile?

Cassandra Vieten: Imagination neurodiversity is the idea that each of us imagines differently, not just in what we imagine, but how, and that this pattern isn't something we're stuck with. Some of this is likely genetic, but at the same time our imagination styles are something we can identify and deliberately shape.

In our lab, we've mapped eighteen different dimensions of imagination that fall into five broader modes. Where you land on each of these results in what we call your imagination profile, your own particular blend of imaginative strengths, tendencies, and blind spots. Some people are vivid visualizers who freeze up when asked to generate a brand-new idea from scratch. Others can conjure incredible sensory detail but struggle to picture their own future. My own profile leans toward being story driven and visually vivid when it comes to fantasy, but I can’t imagine how a piece of furniture might look in a room to save my life.

The point isn't to find the "correct" profile, because there isn't one. It's closer to the paradox we see in other forms of neurodiversity, where a real challenge in one area can sit alongside a genuine strength in another. Once you understand your own profile, you can stop measuring yourself against somebody else's version of "creative" and start working with the imagination you actually have, leaning into what comes easily, and building the muscles that don't. (If you are curious, take a quiz here to learn about your own profile: https://imagination.ucsd.edu/profile/).

Q: How can imagination be developed through practice? What is one specific exercise for readers interested in expanding their imagination?

Cassandra Vieten: While you may have imagination tendencies, it is trainable the same way any other cognitive skill is, through repetition that literally strengthens and rewires the neural connections behind it. In the book I organize the practice side of this into a framework I call VISTA: Visualizing, Ideating, Sensing, Transforming, and Applying. Each is a different way of exercising the imagination on purpose.

If I had to hand a reader just one exercise to start tonight, I'd give them this: pick an important upcoming conversation or situation you are facing, like a hard conversation with a partner, a difficult task at work, or an important interview or presentation. Before it happens, spend two or three minutes picturing it in real detail. Not just the words you'll say, but how you're standing, the tone of your voice, how your shoulders feel, staying loose and steady rather than tight. Walk yourself all the way through it, calm and clear, to the other side.

Here's why this works: your brain doesn't distinguish nearly as much as you'd think between something you vividly imagine and something you're actually experiencing. Brain imaging research shows that when people imagine a threat, the same fear circuitry lights up almost as if it were real, which is exactly why rehearsal like this is so useful. Your nervous system starts laying down some of that groundwork for calm before you ever walk through the door. It costs nothing, needs no equipment, and works anywhere, which is part of why I think of imagination as a genuine health practice, not just a creative one.

Q: What role does imagination play in mental health?

Cassandra Vieten: A much bigger one than most people realize, for better and for worse. I think about mental health on a couple of continuua: the familiar one running from few symptoms to many (anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress), and a second one, mental well-being, running from languishing to flourishing. You can have real symptoms and still be flourishing; you can have no diagnosis and still be languishing. Imagination touches both axes.

On the harmful side, a lot of suffering is really imagination running unsupervised. Catastrophizing, a hallmark of anxiety, involves vivid, detailed imagining of the worst outcome. Depression often comes wrapped in maladaptive storytelling: everyone hates me, I can't do anything right. Those aren't facts, they're narratives your imagination is generating and your mind is mistaking for reality. I know this from the inside, too. I'm a person in recovery from alcoholism, and before I got sober, I imagined constantly that I could stop drinking "tomorrow," that a little rest would fix everything, that telling anyone the truth would cost me their respect. All of it was imagination working against me.

But that same capacity, pointed the other direction, is one of our best tools for healing. Viktor Frankl survived a concentration camp partly by imagining himself, in vivid detail, teaching a lecture hall after the war and reuniting with his wife, using imagination to blow on the secret coals of hope he always held inside. Research on future-oriented interventions has found that helping people with depression and suicidal ideation vividly imagine an attainable, hopeful future can measurably reduce both suicidal thinking and depression scores. The goal isn't to imagine only "positive" things, sometimes rehearsing a hard outcome is exactly what keeps you safe. Even horror films and dystopian novels are ways that society explores what might happen, or what could happen, if we collectively lose our way. The real marker of a healthy imagination is whether it's adaptive: does it help you cope, connect, and function, or does it leave you smaller, more afraid, more alone?

Q: How might therapists utilize imagination in clinical practice?

Cassandra Vieten: More than most clinicians probably give themselves credit for, a lot of our most evidence-based approaches already run on imagination, even when we don't call it that.

In CBT, when a therapist has a client fully imagine a feared scenario in vivid detail, not just a vague fear, but gaming the whole thing out, including the survivable aftermath, and then imagine a best-case and a most-likely scenario alongside it, that's a deliberate use of imagination to dilute a catastrophic narrative. Exposure-based approaches for phobias work the same way: imagined encounters with a feared object, repeated in a safe setting, teach the nervous system that the threat is smaller than it thought. Imagery rescripting, used with painful or traumatic memories, has a strong evidence base for easing emotional suffering.

Then there are approaches that use imagination even more directly. In Gestalt therapy's empty-chair technique, a client imagines a parent, a partner, or a part of themselves sitting across from them and has an actual dialogue, which lets people externalize unfinished business in a way flat conversation rarely reaches. Internal Family Systems, or "parts work," has people imagine their anxiety, their inner critic, or their grief as a character they can actually talk to, get curious about, and hold with compassion instead of fighting. None of these treat imagination as make-believe, they treat it as a real, embodied experience capable of producing real change, because the nervous system responds to a vividly imagined scene almost as if it were happening. For clinicians, I think the invitation is to get more intentional and more literate about a tool that's often already present in the room.

Source: Simon and Schuster/Used with permission

Q: What do you hope readers take away from spending time with Imagine That?

Cassandra Vieten: I hope people close the book believing two things they may not have walked in believing: that their imagination is already unlike anyone else's, and that it's not fixed. It's trainable, ordinary, and theirs to shape.

We're living through what I call the Great Flattening, always plugged in, always managing information, rarely asked to create anything new, with less and less unstructured time to just wonder. That flatness has a cost. I see it as a kind of atrophy, not a permanent condition, and the antidote isn't just telling people to feel more hopeful or more wonder-filled. It's giving them the actual skill of generating hope, and the capacity and tools to re-enchant their own life on purpose. That's the line I keep coming back to: the antidote to despair isn't just hope, it's the skill of generating hope. The antidote to disenchantment isn't just wonder, it's the ability to re-enchant your world, using your imagination.

item.title: Testosterone Testing in the Military Raises New Questions
item.description:
Testosterone

Testosterone Testing in the Military Raises New Questions

Personal Perspective: The real reason for testing troops' testosterone levels.

Posted August 11, 2026

Key points
  • There is no good scientific reason for testing troops' testosterone levels.
  • Hormones affect us, but not in linear fashion; high levels of testosterone don't trigger killer instincts.
  • Screening for low testosterone provides a seemingly objective way to push women out of the military.
Abs by testosterone?
Source: Krzysztof Biernat/Pexels

At the turn of the 21st century, a sociologist from the University of North Carolina published an article claiming that in utero hormones could predict how “feminine” or “masculine” women became as they aged. As a sociologist of gender, I published a critique of his methodology. And I spent years searching for and cleaning the data, and then published an article with Shannon Davis replicating his research, showing that his results were inaccurate, exaggerating the power of hormones sometimes by a factor of 10. It isn’t that in utero hormones don’t matter; it’s just that they don’t matter very much and always matter in complicated interaction with contextual experiences. Much other research has also shown that the relationship between hormones and behavior is complicated and not unidirectional. That is, while hormones may affect behavior, it is also the case that experiences elevate or decrease hormone levels across each and every day.

And yet, here we are in 2026, with the Secretary of Defense (or War) Hegseth announcing that every member of the military, male and female, over the age of 30 must have their testosterone levels monitored. What function does such testing have? Secretary Hegseth claims that soldiers with low testosterone are not top-flight fighters, and so wants to offer hormone treatment to anyone with “too low” testosterone. Let me explain why there is no science behind this claim. And once I’ve shown you that the stated reason doesn’t have any basis in fact, I will propose an alternative hypothesis for this new policy.

Two recent books spar about testosterone and debate its importance in human behavior. In Testosterone: An Unauthorized Biography (Harvard University Press, 2022), the authors Rebecca Jordan-Young and Katrina Karkazis argue that many of the apparent sex differences attributed to hormone levels are the result of biased research, with invalid measures. They argue that testosterone has been mythologized and even fetishized as if it contained quasi-magical properties exclusively related to masculinity. Their review of the research finds that while testosterone matters, it matters much less than heralded, and also varies based on activities.

On the opposite side of this debate, evolutionary biologist Carole Hooven has become famous for defending the notion that sex is a binary and that testosterone matters. She has a TED talk where she makes the case, as well as a book on the topic, T: The Story of Testosterone, the Hormone that Dominates and Divides Us (Henry Holt, 2021). Hooven argues that we too often ignore the importance of testosterone for understanding gender differences in behavior, and her opinion is so controversial that she lost her position at Harvard for speaking on it publicly. Two such opposing experts, however, agree that the actual level of testosterone measured on any given day does not predict combat readiness.

So why isn’t increasing testosterone going to increase the fighting readiness of our troops? First, there are the pragmatic issues. Every person’s testosterone swings daily, and by activities, so to do this effectively, one would have to begin with a study of baseline levels for each soldier over several months or even years. For example, the levels of testosterone in a man’s bloodstream naturally lower when he is an involved father. Do we want to insist that only men who do not procreate enter the military? Similarly, men who engage in violent or competitive activities increase their testosterone levels immediately after. Do we want to ban troops from competition before their testing date? Even more problematic is that every man has a different baseline level, and so you would need to test regularly over several years to be sure when a particular man was low, for his own baseline. And finally, of course, women, on average, have lower testosterone levels than men at every stage of the life cycle; do we really want to experiment on women in the military by artificially increasing their testosterone? We know from anecdotal evidence that women who microdose testosterone in hopes of increasing their energy level notice that it also increases their irritability, as well as their sex drives. One woman quoted in an article in the New York Times claimed she was in a quandary because she was always aroused but so irritated by her husband she couldn’t have sex with him. Do we want a gang of irritable, very horny soldiers?

Another basic problem with the strategy of increasing troops’ testosterone levels is that even if you believe without evidence that an increase in testosterone will make soldiers more aggressive, do you think that what we need in today’s technologically sophisticated warfare are hyperaggressive soldiers ready to slug it out with our enemies? Do we need soldiers guiding drones from afar to be more aggressive or to follow their commanders' orders faithfully? After all, the use of remote-controlled drones already gives soldiers a safety edge over the civilians they may kill with a flick of a switch. Finally, there are many roles in the military where hyperaggression is not even desired, never mind necessary, from medical professionals to support staff.

The claim is that testing every soldier over a certain age for testosterone has no real functional purpose. So why spend money to do it? Why has Hegseth spent political capital pushing for this policy? I have two related hypotheses. First, he is creating a public discourse that presumes men are superior to women, as fighters, as leaders, even as citizens. We shouldn't forget that Hegseth’s pastor doesn’t think women should even have the right to vote. Hegseth is promoting an essentialist belief about gender that promotes male supremacy and misogyny. After all, if you think only people with high levels of testosterone are fit for service, then you can claim to be meritocratic and say anyone who meets this criterion is welcome, simply ignoring the reality that by demanding a certain level of testosterone, you are excluding half the human race. Who can miss the sexism inherent in this project?

But there is a second, and more concrete, purpose to this policy. It justifies Secretary Hegseth’s attempt to push women officers out of the military. In his term in office, he has fired the most senior women from their posts and denied most women and men of color promotions. The most recent data show we have fewer women in leadership in the military than in the past.

So next time you hear about testing soldiers’ testosterone levels, remember that it may be a ruse for pushing women out of the military. It is one step on the road to pushing women out of leadership positions and back into their homes. And if Hegseth follows his pastor’s arguments, the next step is depriving women of their right to vote. Of course, it may be that the Secretary of War would like to be leading an all-male military supporting the United States as a White Christian nation, and this is one step in that direction. And toward tomorrow...

item.title: How to Stop Barking Up the Wrong Tree
item.description:
Denial

How to Stop Barking Up the Wrong Tree

Personal Perspective: How acceptance, instead of denial, promotes well-being.

Posted August 11, 2026

Key points
  • When persistence is no longer productive, pivot to acceptance.
  • Acceptance can foster resilience. Compassion can help us relieve suffering.
  • Tenacity of spirit doesn't mean attaining an impossible goal, but living fiercely through psychological pain.
Source: Tracy Strauss

When we’re dogged, we’re determined. We don’t give up. But sometimes being dogged is as productive as barking up the wrong tree.

Take, for example, my cat, Sam.

In 2010, a Good Samaritan witnessed someone toss a tiny ball of orange fur from a car on the highway. He stopped and rescued this kitten, bringing him to the local Animal Rescue League. With severe head trauma and a degloved lower lip, the team wasn't sure Sam, estimated to be only six or seven weeks old, would survive.

But Sam was dogged.

I was volunteering at the shelter the day after Sam was brought in. I saw him in his cage, his eyes wide with fear. I opened the cage door and placed my hand at the edge as an offering. He leaned his nose forward, sniffed, then crawled into my palm and began purring like a car motor.

Despite what had happened to him at the hands of a human, Sam’s desire to love was dogged.

When he was medically cleared, I adopted him.

Source: Tracy Strauss

Aside from watching birds outside the window, Sam’s favorite pastime was eating. He ate anything and everything. Sometimes I thought he loved food more than he loved me. So when, at the age of 15, he no longer cleaned his bowl, I knew something was wrong. He had kidney disease, a condition without a cure that can cause nausea and distort the sense of taste, among other symptoms as the kidneys fail. By the time a cat displays symptoms, the disease is already quite advanced. The vet recommended I feed Sam prescription food, but Sam wouldn’t eat it. So I bought every kind of cat food I could find. The only thing Sam would eat was Fancy Feast (a rotation of flavors), catnip, and water from a freshly opened can of tuna.

Six months later, he stopped eating the Fancy Feast. He’d sniff at it, then cry, as if begging for food, but he'd eat nothing that I put in front of him. He turned his nose even to cooked chicken and fresh salmon. I poured the water from a fresh can of tuna fish, but he left it. Catnip was moderately appealing, but hardly caloric.

The vet said medication could help. So we tried an anti-nausea pill and a pain pill for the bad arthritis the vet determined he had developed in his back legs. And suddenly, Sam was eating again. He was enjoying his meals and asking for more. He behaved as if he weren't sick. He was more alert and active than he’d been in years. Now that Sam had his quality of life back, I imagined he’d be fine for a very long time.

But three weeks later, Sam stopped eating. He became lethargic. He cried, a lot. He still loved to be brushed, to have the fur just above his nose rubbed, and to sleep with his back up against my spine at night, purring. I told myself there had to be a way to save him, and I would do whatever I could to find a way. Subcutaneous fluids were an option, but Sam didn't tolerate the procedure well, and I knew that forcing him to endure things that scared or otherwise caused him more pain or discomfort was no way for him to live.

Source: Tracy Strauss

What I didn’t want to accept was that Sam was slowly dying, and the end of our life together was near.

What I came to realize was that the more I didn’t accept the truth, the more Sam suffered. In trying to find another way to reverse an irreversible and terminal disease, I was being dogged, but in a way that wasn’t productive or even helpful. I was denying the truth: there was nothing I could do to change the fact of Sam’s decline. In fact, my doggedness was at the expense of Sam’s well-being.

I needed to shift my doggedness away from trying to change what wasn’t possible to change. I had to stop trying to make the reality different.

I believed that acceptance was defeat, but in truth, acceptance can foster resilience.

In accepting Sam’s ultimate decline, I could still be dogged, but in a different way—in my love for him. I could help him transition in as stress-free a way as possible. So I made an end-of-life appointment and a plan for making Sam comfortable in the process. I took a week to shower him with all of his favorite things. On his last day of life, he perked up, ate some Fancy Feast and some water from the tuna can, and he sat in his favorite chair by the window.

In the end, instead of barking up the wrong tree, I gave Sam all the gentle nose rubs he wanted, holding him in my arms as he drifted into sleep.

Source: Tracy Strauss

To be dogged about the wrong thing won’t help you attain your goal—it will only make matters worse. So if you find yourself barking up the wrong tree, ask yourself this: What is the fact or feeling I’m not wanting to accept? Embrace the answer to this question doggedly, releasing suffering with the comfort of compassion.

item.title: You Had So Much Potential. What Went Wrong?
item.description:
Identity

You Had So Much Potential. What Went Wrong?

Recalibrating your expectations can make ambition useful again.

Posted August 11, 2026

Do you ever look at your life and feel that you expected more from it? More excitement, recognition, money, status or freedom? More vaguely, perhaps you expected you to be more.

This is uncomfortable because the missing “more” is difficult to name. You may never have expected a Nobel Prize, a private island or a small but tasteful statue in your hometown. Yet compared with what parents, teachers and your younger self seemed to predict, your present life can feel strangely below forecast.

Perhaps as a child you were good at exams, creative, bold, funny or athletic. These early signs pointed upwards. Surely adult you would be doing rather well.

Then adulthood arrived and stubbornly refused to follow your plotted trajectory.

What Even Is Potential?

Potential is usually inferred from a snapshot. A child performs well in one setting, so we draw an imaginary line from that performance into the distant future. Bright at 12 becomes successful at 30, and top of the class becomes CEO of the company.

But the course of a life is not mapped out by an initial strength or early aptitude. It emerges from a disorderly mixture of ability, personality, judgement, health, resources and unchosen circumstances. Each element changes what happens next, which in turn changes the options, obstacles and opportunities that follow. These effects accumulate across a lifetime, making its course impossible to map in advance.

Potential therefore means something like this: Under an unspecified combination of effort, opportunity and good fortune, you might achieve something impressive. That is probably true of almost everyone, which makes it perilously close to saying nothing.

Telling children they have potential may be intended to encourage effort. Yet there is a difference between “you can improve” and “you are destined to be extraordinary.” Inflated praise can encourage children to see themselves as exceptional rather than simply valued. In one longitudinal study, inflated parental praise predicted greater narcissism among children who already had high self-esteem.

A hopeful message can quietly become a grand prediction. Years later, the prediction becomes an accusation: What happened to you?

When the Prediction Fails

Some people suppress the feeling. They keep busy, drink, seek distraction or insist that they never cared about success. Others take it as a call to action. They work harder, change career, start a business or begin the 100th reinvention of their morning routine.

Others search for an explanation that will let them off the hook. The investigation may lead to their teachers, parents, an unjust society, poor mental health, trauma, previously unrecognised neurodiversity, or almost anything else that can explain why their expected life did not appear.

Some explanations are correct: People really are constrained by illness, discrimination, poor support and missed diagnoses. Such explanations can help us understand recurring difficulties, but may also be used to acquit us of responsibility while protecting the belief that we were exceptional all along.

Adult diagnosis has become much more common. A 2026 UK government review found ADHD and autism diagnoses, referrals and self-identification to be rising much faster than population estimates. A study of more than seven million UK primary-care records found that the rise in ADHD diagnoses between 2000 and 2018 was proportionally greatest among adults. Recorded diagnoses among men aged 18 to 29 increased approximately twentyfold.

The point is not that adult diagnoses are imaginary. It is that “this helps explain a pattern in my life” is very different from “this explains why I am not where I deserve to be.” Even an accurate explanation can be turned into a flattering story.

Your Life Is Not a Controlled Experiment

Feeling behind also requires a comparison. We take another person’s most visible success, perhaps their salary, career, appearance, skills or possessions, and compare it with our private sense of what we might have become.

The comparison is hopelessly contaminated. We cannot hold constant our personalities, health, opportunities or past mistakes. We cannot rerun either life with one variable changed. Nor is there a general leaderboard on which someone is simply “ahead.”

Importantly, we are not even the sole authors of ourselves. None of us chose our starting temperament, intelligence, appearance, parents or appetite for risk. A major meta-analysis of longitudinal research found personality to be both stable and changeable across adulthood. We can change habits and lean towards or away from aspects of ourselves. What we cannot do is perform a complete page-one rewrite of our character.

Our choices matter, but they must bargain with the will of the world. Every plan remains dependent upon events, people and circumstances that sit in the lap of the gods.

Choose What You Now Expect of Yourself

Recalibration does not mean raising or lowering your standards but choosing them more consciously, with some knowledge of your actual strengths, limitations, resources, responsibilities and values.

Stop asking yourself, “What should someone with my potential have achieved by now?” Instead, consider, "Given the person I am and the life I have, what do I reasonably expect of myself? What is my code of conduct? What am I working towards, and what will I leave behind?"

The answers may tell you to try harder, change direction, revive an old ambition or finally abandon one. Research on unattainable goals suggests that, along with persistence, wellbeing depends on our ability to disengage from goals that no longer serve us and commit to new ones.

You may not have wasted your potential. You may simply have outlived a flattering prediction made from inadequate evidence.

Make the most of your life, certainly. Take responsibility for your choices, correct what can be corrected and attempt difficult things. But hold that effort alongside a less comforting truth: The final result was never entirely yours to command.

item.title: Why Myths Still Matter: Did Odysseus Suffer from PTSD?
item.description:
Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder

Why Myths Still Matter: Did Odysseus Suffer from PTSD?

What ancient myths can teach us about psychopathology and therapy today.

Posted August 11, 2026

Key points
  • PTSD isn't new; ancient myths reveal archetypal struggles with trauma and reintegration.
  • Mythic experiences in The Odyssey mirror timeless patterns of psychic numbing and avoidance.
  • Odysseus's distractions with Circe and Calypso parallel modern coping with trauma via escapism.
The Odyssey
Source: Wikimedia Commons

A brief commentary on director Christopher Nolan's new film The Odyssey (2026), in the context of Homer's epic poem and its significance for psychotherapy today: While I am admittedly no movie critic, let me begin by saying that, overall, I did not care much for the film. Not the acting, cinematography, screenwriting, soundtrack, dialog, special effects, nor Nolan's ill-advised casting choices.

Though Matt Damon, an extremely talented actor, is great in the Bourne series and did a superb job playing the deeply traumatized and brilliant young man needing therapy in Good Will Hunting (1997), I did not find him at all convincing as Odysseus for some reason, possibly due to typecasting, though I believe it probably goes well beyond that. While watching the film I kept flashing back to Kirk Douglas as Odysseus in the original 1954 movie version and his far more passionate and nuanced portrayal.

And surprisingly, I also kept imagining Brad Pitt (Achilles in the much better 2004 film Troy ) or some other seasoned action or character actor in the part. Damon just didn't look right to me in the role. Passion, intensity, and complexity, may have been what I found most missing in Matt Damon's rather one-dimensional performance, which was simply too emotionally flat, controlled, and robotic in most scenes, reminiscent of his Jason Bourne character.

Despite his presumably passionate desire and commitment to returning home to Ithaca, his wife, son, and kingdom following a hard-won and bitter victory in the Trojan War, when Odysseus finally finds his way back to his old life after another decade of frustration, loss, and failure, he shows little emotion--anger, joy, relief, love, or sadness--when reuniting with his family and reclaiming his kingdom.

Posing as an itinerant beggar or homeless person upon arrival, it was unclear to me (and others, I suspect) why or how he--and his voice--remained unrecognized for so long by close friends, his son, and especially his devoted wife, Penelope, even when he spoke and his face was not partially hidden by a threadbare hood. In Homer's epic poem The Odyssey, his appearance was magically altered by the goddess Athena, rendering him unrecognizable to anyone other than his old and dying hunting dog.

But this is never adequately explained in Nolan's film, an omission which makes his homecoming scenes incredible--but not in a good way. When Odysseus at last reveals his identity to all by being the only man able to string his old bow and shoot an arrow straight through twelve small openings, he does so without much flair, panache, or drama, turning the climactic scene of the movie, in which he coolly and calculatingly slaughters the would-be-suitors to Queen Penelope--into just another ordinary violent, bloody, battle scene.

But, having said all that, could this tepid performance have been intentional on both the actor's and directors' parts?

Does Odysseus Suffer from PTSD?

If this emotionally detached persona was deliberately written into the script, one possible explanation for it might be that Odysseus was still "shell shocked" by what he witnessed and did during the decade-long war with and violent destruction of Troy, the sort of extreme horrors and exposure to evil that typically lead to symptoms of PTSD in combat soldiers and other trauma survivors. (See my prior post.)

One of those symptoms is what psychiatrist Robert Jay Lifton ( 1986) calls emotional or "psychic numbing." Depression or dissociation is another. It could be said that Damon's Odysseus seems to be objectively and subjectively suffering from such classic symptoms of PTSD seen today including involuntary, intrusive, and distressing memories, flashbacks, and nightmares of deeply traumatic events; recurring efforts to avoid disturbing memories, thoughts, or feelings related to those events; persistent inability to experience positive emotions with flattened or blunted affect; reckless, risky, or self-defeating behavior; and derealization, a pervasive sense of detachment or unreality.

Other than the modern diagnostic terminology, the phenomenon of PTSD is certainly nothing new to the human condition but rather an archetypal pattern of feeling, behavior, and experience affecting some (though not all) people willingly or unwillingly exposed to severe, destructive, and life-threatening experiences of evil like war, mass shootings, and catastrophic natural disasters. (See my prior post.) As with neurosis and psychosis in general, PTSD can profoundly impair reality testing, insight, and judgment.

Indeed, we could speculate that Odysseus, during the course of his ill-fated homeward voyage, may be making what turn out to be very bad decisions that negatively affect not only him but his entire crew because, unconsciously, he does not really want to remember nor return to his previous incarnation, since to do so would require consciously confronting the painfully traumatic reality of the past which he is trying so desperately to forget.

The Defensive Power of Distraction

Odysseus, like the contemporary veteran soldier suffering from PTSD, is truly a wounded hero. Clearly, he does not want to think about what happened, choosing instead to distract himself: first with Circe, the sorceress, next with the beautiful nymph Calypso and then, by deliberately subjecting himself to the seductive (and potentially lethal) song of the Sirens. But knowledge, awareness, or consciousness are the polar opposites of not knowing, unconsciousness, or ignorance, and the last thing the deeply damaged Odysseus seeks.

He craves only oblivion. Unconsciousness. Cessation of suffering. Forgetting. To obliterate the past or future. Perhaps even to die. For Odysseus, these distracting encounters were episodes of erotic, sensual, or sexual intoxication comparable to the abuse of substances such as alcohol, methamphetamine, marijuana, or fentanyl, which frequently co-occurs with PTSD, and can be seen as attempts to temporarily escape from his tormenting and unrelenting inner demons.

And escape Odysseus does, in spades. During his seven lost years with the lovely nymph Calypso (Charlize Theron) she feeds him--and he voluntarily voraciously ingests--lots of opioid-like lotus flowers which cause him to literally forget his past and dream of returning home, succumbing to a state of all-consuming sensual pleasure in the present or here-and-now. (However, in Homer, it was not Odysseus who becomes intoxicated but his crew, whom he then had to rescue.) In any case, distraction can manifest in myriad ways major and minor, such as misadventures, aggression, substance use, pornography, gambling, and risky behavior, a tendency toward hyperstimulation we typically see in PTSD patients, some of whom, like Odysseus, have extraordinary difficulty finding their way home, i.e., returning to civilian life or to their former ways of being in the world.
